name: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
statusNote: The Senate passed it 62 to 33 on November 19, 2026. The House has not voted on the Senate version, and no House vote date was set as of November 23. It is not law.

changes.title: Federal agencies get a clock
changes.felt: Power lines, pipelines, mines and other projects that need federal sign-off would get answers on a schedule instead of waiting years.
changes.who: Anyone near a proposed project, and anyone waiting on one to be built.

numbers.label: to finish a shorter environmental review (an EA)
to finish a full environmental impact statement

changes.mechanics: Section 1106 sets deadlines for agency decisions: 1 year for an environmental assessment and 2 years for an environmental impact statement, then 90 days (or 120 for agencies outside the review) to decide on permits. Missed deadlines bring consequences for senior officials, and the developer can go to court over a missed deadline. Section 1403, per the CRS summary of the introduced bill, gives permits that need no environmental review a 1 year decision deadline.

changes.title: 150 days to challenge a project in court
changes.felt: If you think a project near you skipped a proper environmental review, you or a group you back would have about five months to sue, and the case starts in a federal appeals court.
changes.who: Neighbors, tribes, local governments and groups that challenge projects, and the companies building them.

numbers.label: to file after the approval is made public

changes.mechanics: Section 1110 adds a new NEPA section 111. A claim must be filed within 150 days after the environmental impact statement is published in the Federal Register or the approval is made public, in a federal court of appeals. The person suing must claim direct harm and, for comment periods held after the law takes effect, must have filed a detailed comment. See Who's worried and why for what this means in practice.

changes.title: A flawed review usually would not stop the project
changes.felt: Even if a court agrees the review was flawed, the project could generally keep going while the agency fixes the paperwork.
changes.who: Same as above. This changes what winning a lawsuit gets you.
changes.mechanics: Section 1110 makes sending the review back to the agency, without canceling the permit or ordering work to stop, the only remedy for a NEPA violation. The permit stays in effect during the fix, which the court can require within 180 days. Courts must give the agency substantial deference. A court can still pause a project early if it is likely breaking a law other than NEPA or the historic preservation law.

changes.title: Developers could sue over bad-faith denials
changes.felt: If a court finds the government blocked a project in bad faith, taxpayers could owe the developer a large share of its costs.
changes.who: Developers, and taxpayers who would fund any payments.
changes.mechanics: Per the Congressional Research Service summary of the bill as introduced: Section 1401 bars agencies from revoking or changing a fully permitted project's approvals unless the agency proves an exception by clear and convincing evidence, and a court finding of bad faith adds a payment of 25 to 50 percent of costs. Section 1402 lets a developer sue over a pattern of denials or delays for its type of project, with a win paying 50 to 100 percent of expected construction cost. Payments come from the Judgment Fund, which needs no new vote in Congress. A tracker reports the same ranges in the passed text. See Who's worried and why.

changes.title: A federal backup for big power lines
changes.felt: Long power lines that cross state lines could get a federal path to approval when states do not act.
changes.who: People who pay electric bills, and landowners along proposed routes.
changes.mechanics: Section 2101 changes transmission permitting and, per the CRS summary of the introduced bill, gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission backstop siting authority for some interstate lines. Some senators proposed amendments to narrow it (for example, giving states two years first). We have not confirmed how the passed text handles this.

changes.title: Data centers pay for the grid they need
changes.felt: The bill aims to keep the cost of serving big data centers off other customers’ electric bills.
changes.who: Anyone with an electric bill in an area where data centers are being built.
changes.mechanics: Section 2107 is titled "Ratepayer protection." A law firm reading the Senate substitute reported that it makes large new loads cover both new and existing transmission costs they cause, and that the substitute dropped a 20 megawatt threshold. We have not read the section’s text ourselves, so treat the details as reported.

changes.title: Changes to historic and sacred site reviews
changes.felt: Tribes say the bill weakens their say when projects could harm sacred sites. Sponsors say it strengthens consultation. See Who's worried and why for the details.
changes.who: Tribal nations, and communities with historic places near projects.
changes.mechanics: The bill's historic preservation title (Sec. 2301) rewrites how agencies review effects on historic and sacred places under Section 106. Tribal groups and analysts report set response deadlines, softer consultation wording and fewer projects covered. The substitute dropped a federal redefinition of tribal sacred places and an Interior takeover of tribal preservation offices. We have not read this title's text.

myths.claim: It passed, so it is law.
myths.fact: Not yet. The House has to pass the same text, then the President has to sign it.
It started as one. The Senate replaced its text with BAAJA on November 18 and kept the original tax provision, on damages paid to abuse survivors, as Division C.
S. 5653 is the original Senate bill and has had no action since September 30. The live version is H.R. 2347.

myths.claim: It will cut your power bill by a set amount.
myths.fact: No official estimate of the effect on power bills exists. Lower bills are a claim by supporters, not a measured result.

myths.claim: It is just about faster energy permits.
myths.fact: It also changes mining law on public land, rewrites historic and sacred site reviews, limits lawsuits, and protects issued permits from later changes.

concernsIntro: Tribal nations, environmental groups, some state and local officials and some members of Congress say parts of this bill go well beyond speeding up permits. Here is each worry: who raises it, what it could mean in practice, what we could confirm in the bill, and what supporters say back. Each one is labeled by how solid it is.

concerns.title: Tribes say they would lose real say over sacred sites
concerns.short: Rewritten historic site reviews could let a project move ahead before a tribe can identify a sacred place.

critics.who: National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers

concerns.claim: Title III rewrites Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, the step where federal agencies must consult tribes before a project can harm historic or sacred places. As tribal groups and analysts read it: the duty softens to agencies having to "seek, discuss, as appropriate, and incorporate, as applicable" tribal views; tribes face set deadlines, including 30 days to respond to an agency report, after which the agency may go ahead; projects whose only federal role is a grant or loan would generally skip the review, except Transportation Department projects over $10 million; and tribal preservation offices would face federal performance reviews that can suspend their funding. NCAI says the changes "strip the protections to sacred sites that Tribal Nations have relied on for 60 years."

quote.text: Once these places are bulldozed, they cannot be restored.
quote.who: Ira L. Matt, executive director, National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers

concerns.practice: Many sacred places are not on any public map, and tribes often keep their locations private for protection. A tribal preservation office with one or two staff can get many review requests at once. Under a 30-day clock, a missed deadline lets the agency move on, and a tribal policy explainer says the agency would not have to revisit earlier findings if the tribe comes back later. Add the 150-day lawsuit window and the limits on stopping a project in court, and a tribe that spots harm late may have little it can still do.
concerns.confirmed: In the part of the substitute text we read, the environmental review title adds two protections for tribes: a NEPA lawsuit over a project on tribal trust land can generally be brought only by that tribe, and when a tribe proposes its own project, agencies must presume that saying no would hurt the tribe. Those are not in the historic preservation title tribes object to.
concerns.open: We have not read Title III's text, so the deadlines and wording above are the critics' reading. A tribal policy explainer and NCAI say the substitute dropped two earlier pieces tribes fought: a federal redefinition of tribal sacred places and an Interior Department takeover of tribal preservation offices. Whether floor changes on November 17 and 18 touched the 30-day clock is not confirmed.

response.who: Sen. Mike Lee, a lead sponsor, on the Senate floor
response.claim: "We have strengthened Tribal consultation provisions." Sen. Martin Heinrich, another sponsor, says the bill is defending against the administration's attacks on tribal consultation.

concerns.title: Less time and fewer ways to challenge a project in court
concerns.short: 150 days to sue, only if you commented, and even a win usually cannot stop construction.

critics.who: National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers
Rep. Adelita Grijalva and other House Democrats

concerns.claim: Critics say the bill shuts most people out of court. Earthjustice says challenges that can now be filed for up to six years would have to be filed within 150 days. NRDC says a court "can never invalidate a permit" over a violation of the environmental review law or the historic preservation law. Rep. Adelita Grijalva says the bill would "all but eliminate judicial review."
concerns.practice: Say a company gets approval for a pipeline or a mine near a small town or a reservation. The clock starts when the approval is made public. Residents who learn about it late, who did not file a detailed comment during the comment period, or who cannot show direct harm may not be able to sue at all. Those who can sue start in a federal appeals court, which costs more than a local trial court. If they win, the agency redoes its review, in up to 180 days, and the permit stays in effect, so work can keep going. The bill also bars any claim over who a developer left off its required outreach list of state, local and tribal officials.
concerns.confirmed: We read this in the sponsors' November 7 substitute text: the 150-day deadline; the rule that you must have filed a substantive comment, for comment periods held after the law takes effect; the direct-harm test; appeals-court venue; remand without vacatur or injunction as the only remedy; the permit staying in effect during remand; substantial deference to the agency; and no claims over omissions from the developer's outreach list. A court can still pause a project early if it is likely breaking a law other than NEPA or the historic preservation law.
concerns.open: We have not read how the same limits apply to historic preservation claims under Sec. 2301. Earthjustice and NATHPO say they do.

response.who: Sen. Martin Heinrich, a lead sponsor
response.claim: "We make permitting faster, and so we're going to be able to put more cheap, clean electrons onto the grid."

concerns.title: Taxpayers could owe developers if a permit is pulled
concerns.short: Approved permits get hard to revoke, and bad-faith interference could cost taxpayers 25 to 100 percent of a project's costs.

critics.who: Eight California mayors and county supervisors

concerns.claim: Critics say Sec. 1401 freezes permits once issued for any project with a private sponsor, including mines, logging and data centers, not only clean energy. The Clean Air Task Force says it creates "a risk that it would be difficult for future administrations to unwind hastily issued or unlawful permits." California local officials warn Sec. 1402 could mean "billions in taxpayer-funded damages."
concerns.practice: If a later administration decides a permit was a mistake and tries to pull or tighten it, the agency has to prove by clear and convincing evidence that one of a short list of exceptions applies. If a court finds the government acted in bad faith, the developer can collect 25 to 50 percent of its costs. Under Sec. 1402, a developer can sue if approvals for its type of project dropped sharply compared with the past five years, and collect 50 to 100 percent of expected construction costs. Payments come from the Judgment Fund, a standing account that needs no vote in Congress. CRS notes about $3.8 billion was paid from it for 10 offshore wind settlements from April to October 2026.
concerns.confirmed: The Congressional Research Service describes these mechanics in the bill as introduced (report R49511, November 6, 2026): the clear and convincing standard, the payment ranges and the Judgment Fund. CRS says Sec. 1402 "appears to contemplate a finding of liability without any direct evidence" of intent. The Institute for Progress says the substitute moved the protected date from September 16 to November 6, 2026.
concerns.open: We have not read Title IV in the passed text. Lawyers disagree about how far the lock-in reaches.

response.claim: "Section 1401 restricts federal agencies, not courts." The government can still ask a court to cancel an unlawful permit, and the 25 to 50 percent payment needs a court finding of bad faith.

concerns.title: Mines could put waste on more public land
concerns.short: Critics say mining companies could claim public land for waste rock and tailings with no acreage limit.
concerns.claim: Critics say Sec. 2215 removes the acreage limits on mining "mill sites" and lets companies use public land for waste rock, tailings and "any other use relevant to a mining project," in NRDC's words. Earthworks says companies could claim "nearly unlimited public lands." Earthjustice and Heatmap News say it would reverse a 2022 federal appeals court ruling that stopped the Rosemont copper mine in Arizona.
concerns.practice: Public land next to a mine, including land used for hunting, grazing or tribal cultural practices, could be covered by waste piles for decades, and cleanup can fall to taxpayers if a company walks away.
concerns.confirmed: The bill's table of contents lists Sec. 2215, "Hardrock mining mill sites." Heatmap News reported in October that the bill includes the full text of the Mining Regulatory Clarity Act.
concerns.open: We have not read Sec. 2215's text, so the details are the critics' reading.

noResponse.text: We found no sponsor statement on this section. Earthworks, a critic, called the bill's abandoned mine cleanup fund "the one good thing" it had spotted, to Heatmap News.

concerns.title: Some pipelines and loan-backed projects skip environmental review
concerns.short: Certain gas pipeline work and projects backed only by federal loans would not count as federal actions that need review.
concerns.claim: Critics say the bill quietly narrows which projects get any environmental review. Earthjustice says "pipeline expansions within existing rights-of-way" and projects backed only by federal loans or loan guarantees would be excluded. NRDC says states and tribes would lose power over a gas pipeline's water impacts other than direct discharges, and that many oil and gas wells on private land would no longer need federal permits.
concerns.practice: When a project is not a "major federal action," there is no environmental assessment, no impact statement and no NEPA comment period, so neighbors may first hear about it when work starts. Fewer reviews also means fewer decisions anyone can challenge.
concerns.confirmed: In the substitute text (Sec. 1102), the definition of major federal action leaves out projects with no or minimal federal funding, projects whose only federal role is a loan or loan guarantee, natural gas pipeline "covered activities" defined in a new section of the Natural Gas Act, and certain transmission work. Sec. 1106 also makes the White House Council on Environmental Quality's ruling on disputes between agencies final, with no court review.
concerns.open: We have not read the new Natural Gas Act section, so we have not confirmed exactly which pipeline work counts. The water and private-land well claims (Secs. 1202 and 2211) are the critics' reading.

response.claim: "By streamlining environmental reviews and permitting procedures, this legislation will help lower energy costs."

concession.text: NRDC, which opposes the bill, also says faster permitting "may not produce a large increase in emissions compared with business as usual."

concerns.title: Washington could approve a power line a state rejected
concerns.short: Federal regulators could approve an interstate line after a state says no or takes more than a year.

critics.who: No 765 Line, a Wisconsin group fighting a proposed line

concerns.claim: The Wisconsin group says Sec. 2101 lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approve an interstate line after the state utility commission says no, takes more than a year, or sets conditions that make the line "not economically feasible." It says FERC must weigh landowners' views, but "None of these rules lets a landowner or the state stop a FERC permit."
concerns.practice: Landowners along a route would have less leverage through their own state. Whether a federal permit would carry the power to take land by eminent domain matters a lot for them, and we could not confirm it in the passed text.
concerns.confirmed: CRS describes backstop siting authority for FERC in the bill as introduced.
concerns.open: We have not read Sec. 2101's text and have not confirmed any eminent domain power.

response.who: NRDC, which opposes the bill overall
response.claim: Calls the transmission and interconnection reforms "the bill's principal strengths." Earthjustice also calls the transmission provisions very positive.

concerns.title: Data center rules cover grid costs, not local impacts
concerns.short: Data centers would pay for grid upgrades, but the bill leaves their water use, noise and air pollution alone.
concerns.claim: NRDC supports the grid cost provisions but says "The bill does not address local air pollution, water consumption, noise, land use."
concerns.practice: A town that hosts a data center might be spared some electric bill increases, but water use, diesel backup generators and noise stay with state and local rules.
concerns.confirmed: The table of contents lists Sec. 2107, "Ratepayer protection," and Sec. 2117, a Data Center Community Assistance Program.
concerns.open: We have not read either section's text.

response.who: Sen. Martin Heinrich, a lead sponsor
response.claim: The bill will "make sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause."
